reason: A five-word run and the chapter's top-ranked candidate at this verse, and it is the Book of Mormon's own standing phrase. 'Upon all the face of the earth/land' runs through the whole book from 1 Nephi onward and is covered by the standing exclusion filed in 1 Nephi; Ezekiel 34:6's scattered flock has nothing else in common with a voice heard after an earthquake. The verse's real business is the voice itself, which is adjudicated at 9:2 against Revelation 8:13.

A tempting candidate and very nearly the right one. “devil and his angels” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:41, where they are the party for whom the everlasting fire was prepared — and 3 Nephi 9 has just burned four cities with fire. But the Book of Mormon's clause is 'the Devil laugheth, and his angels rejoice', and the verb is what decides it: Revelation 12:12 has the devil, the woe, the inhabiters of the earth and the rejoicing all in one verse, and 3 Nephi 9:2 has all four. Matthew 25:41 supplies only the possessive. The link is written at 9:2 against Revelation 8:13 with Revelation 12:12 composite; Matthew is recorded here because a reader who knows the singleton will expect to find it cited.

The phrase is this chapter's refrain — it occurs at 9:5, 9:6, 9:7 (three times), 9:8 and 9:10 — and it is King James boilerplate for a city and its population, which the machine ranked only because the surrounding words happened to align. Micah 6:12, proposed at 9:8 for the same string, falls with it. Neither Isaiah's grasshoppers nor Micah's liars has any further contact with a list of destroyed Nephite cities. This entry covers every 'and the inhabitants thereof' candidate in the chapter.

“the depths of the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, which is why it ranked twice in this chapter (9:6 and 9:8), and the sense runs the opposite way. Psalm 71:20 is a prayer of confidence: 'thou … shalt quicken me again, and shalt bring me **up** again from the depths of the earth.' The depths there are the place God rescues a man out of, and the whole force of the verse is the ascent. 3 Nephi 9:6 and 9:8 use the same phrase for the descent — cities and their inhabitants 'buried up in the depths of the earth' so that their wickedness may never come up again. A singleton is strong evidence of a source only when the borrowing does something a reader of the source would recognise, and here the borrowing would have to reverse the one thing the psalm asserts. The chapter's word for what is buried is 'hid', and the psalm hides nothing.

“hills and valleys” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the temptation is that both verses are about the shape of a promised land. Deuteronomy 11:11 is the contrast drawn between Egypt, watered by foot, and Canaan, 'a land of hills and valleys' that drinks the rain of heaven — the topography is the blessing, evidence that God tends the land directly. 3 Nephi 9:8 makes hills and valleys by burying four cities and their inhabitants, so that the terrain is the grave and the erasure of a record. Same two nouns, opposite theology of landscape, and no third word shared. Recorded because the singleton is real and a reader will find it.

The highest-scoring machine candidate at 9:9 and again at 9:10, on a six-word run. “burned with fire” occurs in exactly seventeen KJV verses and is the King James Bible's ordinary description of a destroyed city — Jerusalem's gates at Nehemiah 1:3 and 2:17, the cities of Isaiah 1:7, Ziklag at 1 Samuel 30:3. Jeremiah 38:23 is Zedekiah being told he will cause Jerusalem to be burned, which is a warning to a king about his own city and not a divine announcement of completed judgement. Where this chapter's burning does have a source it is Revelation 18:8, 'she shall be utterly burned with fire', which is adjudicated at 9:3 with the rest of the Babylon cluster.

“more righteous than” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, and Ezekiel 16:52 is the only one that is a divine judgement oracle rather than a private admission (Genesis 38:26, 1 Samuel 24:17) or a complaint (Habakkuk 1:13). It is also full of this chapter's other keyword: 'thy sins that thou hast committed more abominable than they.' But the comparison is inverted at the point that matters. Ezekiel tells Jerusalem that Sodom and Samaria 'are more righteous than thou' — the comparative is an accusation levelled at the survivor. 3 Nephi 9:13 tells the survivors 'ye were more righteous than they', and uses the comparative as the reason they are alive. An identical construction doing the opposite work.

Five words of pure conditional syntax, and the top machine candidate at this verse. Genesis 34:15 is Jacob's sons setting the terms of Shechem's circumcision; nothing but the grammar of a conditional offer is shared. The same applies to Deuteronomy 15:11's 'of the land therefore' at 9:9. Listed once for both.

Worth recording because of what stands four verses later. 3 Nephi 9:18 quotes ten words of Revelation 22:13, and Revelation 22:17 — four verses on in the source — reads 'And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely', which sits close to 9:14's 'whosoever will come, him will I receive'. If the chapter were working through the end of Revelation in order, this would be the second stop. It is not enough: “whosoever will” occurs in exactly eleven KJV verses and is a bare relative construction, the Book of Mormon adds 'come' where Revelation has 'take', and there is no water, no thirst and no freely. The Alpha and Omega quotation at 9:18 stands on its own wording and does not need a neighbour.

reason: A six-word run and a real influence on the wording, but not the source of its grammar. Nehemiah 9:6 reads 'the earth, and all things that **are** therein', which is idiomatic and which the Book of Mormon does not have. The 1830 reads 'all things that in them **is**' — a singular verb on a plural antecedent, which is a King James solecism occurring in exactly two verses, Exodus 20:11 and Acts 4:24. Nehemiah probably supplies 'things'; Exodus and Acts supply the construction, and the link is written there. Recorded here because the machine ranks Nehemiah and a reader working from the 1920 text, where 'is' has been corrected to 'are', will find Nehemiah the better fit — which is precisely the effect CONVENTIONS §8 warns about.

The expectation is strong enough to need answering. This chapter is a voice out of darkness that identifies itself six times in eight verses — 'I am Jesus Christ', 'I am in the Father', 'I am the light and the life of the world', 'I am Alpha and Omega' — and the reader's ear goes to Exodus 3:14, the burning-bush self-naming and the Bible's foundational divine 'I am'. The wording will not bear it. Exodus 3:14 reads 'I AM THAT I AM … Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you', where the formula is absolute: the predicate of 'I am' is 'I am'. Every one of this chapter's formulas is predicated in the ordinary way — I am *X* — which is the construction of John's self-predications and of Revelation's, and both of those are present with their own verbatim wording (John 14:10 at 9:15, John 8:12 at 9:18, Revelation 22:13 at 9:18). There is no shared word beyond the copula, and the copula is not evidence. Recorded so that a reader who came to this chapter looking for Exodus 3 is told the catalogue looked too.

reason: The best-known of Revelation's four self-identifications and the one most readers name, and it is excluded by a single syllable. Revelation 1:8 reads 'the beginning and the **ending**'; 3 Nephi 9:18 reads 'the beginning and the end', which occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 21:6 and 22:13. The link is written at 9:18 against Revelation 22:13 with 21:6 composite. This entry also discharges the Frederick row at this verse: `data/frederick-refs.json` records Revelation 1:8 as occurring near his discussion of 3 Nephi 9:18, which is a fact about the index's co-occurrence window and not a source proposal by him — his subject is the Gospel of John. Our reading places the wording at 21:6/22:13, and the difference is one word long and checkable.

The exclusion a reader is most likely to dispute, so it is written out. Psalm 51:16-17 is the Bible's classic preference of contrition over sacrifice — 'thou desirest not sacrifice … The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise' — and 3 Nephi 9:19-20 makes exactly that argument, abolishing sacrifice and substituting the broken heart. On subject matter Psalm 51 is unanswerable. On wording it is wrong, and the wording is what this catalogue records. Psalm 51:17 pairs the adjectives with the opposite nouns: broken *spirit*, contrite *heart*. 3 Nephi 9:20 has 'a broken heart and a contrite spirit', and “broken heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — Psalm 34:18 — which also carries “contrite spirit” and carries the two in this order. The link is written at 9:20 against Psalm 34:18; Psalm 51 is where the thought comes from and Psalm 34 is where the words do.

The top two machine candidates at this verse, Acts 15:8 and Acts 4:31, both rank on the phrase 'the Holy Ghost' plus whatever happens to follow it. Acts 15:8's 'giving them the Holy Ghost, even as he did unto us' is Peter defending the Gentile mission at the Jerusalem council; the 'even as' that produced the match is the Book of Mormon's own comparative introducing the Lamanites, not a borrowed clause. Acts 4:31 shares only 'with the Holy Ghost'. The verse's real New Testament source is the Baptist's saying at Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16, adjudicated at 9:20.
